title: Eugene Clean Energy Fund Leads Early Returns on Election Night
dek: Measure 20-388 would charge large retailers and banks a licensing fee of 2% of their Eugene gross profits to fund clean energy projects; early results on Tuesday showed about 58% support.
author: Meridian Newsroom

body:
Early returns in Eugene, Oregon, show voters leaning toward a new clean energy fund, with the measure ahead on election night. KLCC reported that about 58% of tallied votes favored the Eugene Clean Energy Fund as of 11 p.m. Pacific time on Tuesday. These are initial returns, and the final count will determine the outcome.

## What the measure would do

Measure 20-388 would require some large retailers and banks to pay a new annual licensing fee equal to 2% of their gross profits in the city. The revenue would be spent on clean energy projects. KLCC reports that the fee requirement would take effect in 2029 if the measure passes.

The proposal is modeled on a similar policy Portland voters approved in 2018, according to the campaign's co-chief petitioners. Supporters argue that the largest companies doing business in Eugene should contribute more to local climate resilience.

## The campaign

The campaign raised more than $730,000, according to KLCC. Canvassers said they knocked on about 26,000 doors, and households received online advertising and mailers in the final weeks. Co-chief petitioner Aya Cockram said the result showed the community is ready for change.

Opponents, led by the Stop the Hidden Tax on Eugene campaign, argued the fee would be passed on to customers and that the revenue could be misused. Their reported fundraising was about $155,000 as of Monday. In a statement Tuesday night, the group said its concerns about affordability and accountability remain unchanged, and urged city leaders to take them seriously during implementation.

## What is still unknown

The early count does not settle the measure. Final certified results will show whether the lead holds as later ballots are tallied. The article does not establish how many companies would pay the fee, or how much revenue it would raise, because those figures were not part of the reporting reviewed here.

The measure also leaves open how the fund would be governed. Opponents questioned accountability, and supporters have not yet described the fund's administration in the coverage cited here.

## Why it matters

Local clean-energy funding measures are one way cities try to pay for climate work without relying only on state or federal money. A fee tied to gross profits, rather than sales or property, would reach companies of a certain size directly. If Eugene approves it, the policy would be one of the more concrete local tests of whether that model can pass at the ballot box outside Portland.

Meridian will update this story if certified results or a city implementation schedule are published.
